title: Divide, Parse, Enclose
focus: Last day of new material. Merge sort earning its keep, a parser you can defend, and the last flood fill.

cards.title: Merge Sort and Counting
cards.trigger: Counting pairs across a whole array where a naive double loop is quadratic.
cards.recall: Write merge sort from memory, then add the counting line. Then answer: at the moment you take an element from the right half, what have you learned about the remaining left half?
useWhen: Count inversions in an array
Reverse pairs, count of smaller numbers after self
Sort a linked list in O(n log n) with O(log n) space
Any pair-counting reducible to a merge step
Where you need a guaranteed n log n and stability
template: while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
# left[i..] are ALL greater than right[j], so they all invert with it
# Linked list merge sort: split with fast/slow, sort halves, merge with a dummy.
keyInsights: Both halves are already sorted at merge time, so one comparison settles a whole block of pairs at once
`<=` rather than `<` is what makes the sort stable, and stability matters when elements carry payloads
Reverse pairs needs a separate counting pass before the merge, because the condition is not the merge comparison
cards.trap: 'Why not a Fenwick tree?' You can, after coordinate compression, and it is the same complexity. Being able to give both, and say which you would ship, is the strong answer.

cards.title: Expression Parsing
patterns: Push result and sign on open
cards.trigger: Evaluate an expression string with parentheses or precedence, without using eval.
cards.recall: Write the plus-minus-parentheses calculator from memory. Then answer the key modelling choice: what two values do you push onto the stack when you hit an open parenthesis?
useWhen: Basic calculator, with and without multiplication
Evaluate reverse Polish notation
Decode string, simplify path, the same stack family
Any grammar shallow enough to parse without a real parser
Nested boolean or arithmetic evaluation
template: # Plus, minus, parentheses. Sign is carried, not stored as an operator.
stack.append(total); stack.append(sign)   # park the outer context
total *= stack.pop()                      # the sign before the '('
total += stack.pop()                      # the total before the '('
# With * and /: keep a running stack of TERMS, and fold * and / immediately,
# then sum the stack at the end. Precedence handled by when you fold.
keyInsights: Pushing the total and the sign is exactly the same frame idea as decode string. One family, two dressings
Handling the trailing number after the loop is mandatory, because there is no operator to trigger the final flush
Precedence is decided by when you fold, not by a precedence table. Multiplication folds immediately, addition folds at the end
cards.trap: 'Add unary minus and spaces.' Spaces are a skip, unary minus needs the sign initialised per context. Both are small, and both break a solution that assumed clean input.

cards.title: Prefix Sums on a Tree
patterns: Undo the map entry on the way out
cards.trigger: Count downward paths with a given sum, where paths need not start at the root.
cards.recall: Write path sum III in O(n) from memory. Then answer: this is exactly the Day 4 array trick. What is the one extra line the tree version needs, and what breaks without it?
useWhen: Path sum III, count paths with a target sum
Longest path with a divisible or bounded sum
Count paths with a given XOR value
Any array prefix technique lifted onto a tree
Where the naive per-node restart would be O(n^2)
template: prefix[0] = 1                 # the empty prefix, same seed as the array version
keyInsights: The undo is the only difference from the array version. Without it, a right subtree counts prefixes that exist only in the left subtree
`prefix[0] = 1` handles paths that begin at the root, exactly as in the array case
The naive version, restarting a DFS at every node, is O(n^2) or O(n log n) on a balanced tree. This is linear
cards.trap: 'The path can go up and back down.' Prefix sums along a root path do not cover that. It becomes a record-versus-return problem instead. Confirm the direction before coding.

cards.title: Bottom-Up Accumulation
patterns: Fill from the last row upward
cards.trigger: A layered structure where each cell chooses among a small set of successors in the next layer.
cards.recall: Write the triangle solution bottom-up from memory. Then answer: why is bottom-up cleaner than top-down here, in terms of how many boundary cases each has?
useWhen: Triangle minimum path total
Minimum falling path sum
Any layered DAG shortest path with local moves
Dungeon game and other suffix-constrained grids
Where the goal is a single cell but the start is a whole row, or vice versa
template: # dp[c] = best total from row r, column c, down to the bottom
dp = triangle[-1][:]                    # start with the bottom row
# Top-down needs boundary handling at c == 0 and c == r on every row.
# Bottom-up needs none, because dp[c] and dp[c+1] always exist.
# Minimum falling path sum: same shape, but three neighbours,
# and the ends need a guard because the grid is rectangular.
keyInsights: Bottom-up has zero boundary cases here, because row r has r+1 cells and row r+1 has r+2. That asymmetry is the whole reason to go upward
One array of state is enough, since each row reads only the row below
Choosing the direction of a DP is a design decision, not a preference. Pick whichever removes the special cases
cards.trap: 'Do it in O(1) extra space.' You can mutate the triangle in place. Say that it destroys the input, which is a real cost if the caller reuses it.

cards.title: Border-Anchored Flood Fill
cards.trigger: Everything not connected to the outside gets transformed.
cards.recall: Write surrounded regions from memory. Then answer the strategic question: why is it far simpler to find what SURVIVES than to find what is enclosed?
useWhen: Surrounded regions, number of enclaves, closed islands
Count regions not touching the boundary
Escape-the-grid reachability
Any 'enclosed by' or 'cannot reach the outside' question
Where checking each region for enclosure separately would be quadratic
template: if r < 0 or r >= rows or c < 0 or c >= cols or board[r][c] != 'O':
# 1. anything reachable from the border survives
# 2. everything else was enclosed; restore the survivors
keyInsights: Enclosure is a global property and hard to test locally. Border-reachability is local and easy, so invert the question
The temporary marker must be a third symbol. Reusing 'X' loses the information you are about to need
On a large grid the recursion depth is the whole grid. Convert to an explicit stack and say why
cards.trap: 'Closed island, where zeros are land.' Same technique, inverted values, and now the border cells you flood are land rather than water. Read which symbol is which.
